summary: Describes the IANA table that says how X.400 message body part types match MIME content types, and sets up its initial contents. New mappings were meant to be registered with IANA to avoid duplicates. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1494 defines a table for matching X.400 message body parts to MIME content types. It also describes how gateways can copy, convert, or encapsulate content when transferring it between the two mail systems.

subtitle: A mapping table for converting X.400 and MIME message body types.

tldr.problem: Mail gateways connecting X.400 and MIME-based message systems need a shared way to identify equivalent body types and the conversion required between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an IANA equivalence table with entries for an X.400 body part, a MIME content type, a conversion type, and optional comments, and it provides initial mappings.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1494 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It was written as a companion to RFC 1495, which describes the broader interworking principles.

today: RFC 1494 is Historic according to the unit metadata, which lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It was written as a companion to RFC 1495.

sections.title: Purpose of the Equivalence Table
sections.content:
RFC 1494 is a companion to RFC 1495, which describes principles for interworking between MIME-based RFC 822 mail and X.400. This document defines the contents and initial configuration of the IANA MHS/MIME Equivalence table.

MIME calls an information object in a message body a content type, while X.400 calls it a body part type. RFC 1494 uses the term body part for either. It says mappings for new content types or body part types should be registered with IANA to reduce duplication and support interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The table matches names used by X.400 with names used by MIME for message content. A gateway can consult the matching entry when moving content between the systems.

sections.title: Table Entries and Conversion Types
sections.content:
Each table entry identifies the X.400 body part, the MIME content type, and a conversion type; it may also contain comments. The MIME content type must already be registered with IANA. The RFC defines four conversion types.

  • Byte copy copies the byte stream without conversion and is the preferred method.
  • Text conversion scans and reformats text when encodings or line and page breaks differ.
  • Image conversion reformats raster image data at the pixel level.
  • Tunneling encapsulates the object when no explicit mapping applies.
sections.plainLanguage: An entry tells a gateway whether to copy content unchanged, reformat text, reformat an image, or encapsulate content. Byte copy is preferred when the formats permit it.

sections.title: Mappings for Content Without a Pair
sections.content:
The RFC defines X.400 Extended Body Parts identified by object identifiers under a shared OID tree. A generic MIME Extended Body Part can carry a MIME content type for which there is no registered mapping, along with its parameters and original content bytes.

In the other direction, the MIME type application/x400-bp carries an X.400 body part that has no registered mapping. Other mappings in the RFC include text, ODA, PostScript, JPEG, GIF, and Group 3 facsimile. The fax mapping uses a sequence of six end-of-line markers to separate pages.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines generic containers for content that has no specific table entry. It also gives mappings for selected text, document, image, and fax formats.

sections.title: Registering New Mappings
sections.content:
The RFC provides a registration form for new mappings. It asks for the MIME type, X.400 body part, object identifiers, ASN.1 syntax, conversion algorithm, and a contact. If an object identifier is not supplied, IANA assigns one under the relevant subtree.

The conversion algorithm must be specified completely enough for independent implementation, or may be defined by reference to an RFC. The Security Considerations section states that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A new mapping needs a defined content type, body part, and conversion method. The RFC says that it does not discuss security issues.
